enonce_markdown: A seamstress in a workshop in Bafoussam is paid 800 FCFA for every shirt she sews. This method of wage payment is called:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A time rate pays for time worked; a piece rate pays for each unit of output produced.

### Solution

Her pay depends on the number of shirts she completes, not on the hours she works. This is a **piece rate**. A time rate would be a fixed amount per hour or day, a salary is a fixed monthly amount, and overtime is extra pay for hours beyond the normal week. **Answer: B.**

enonce_markdown: A bricklayer leaves Garoua to take a job on a building site in Yaounde. This is an example of:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Geographical mobility of labour is the ability to move from one place to another to work; occupational mobility is the ability to change from one type of job to another.

### Solution

The worker changes **location** but not occupation, so this is **geographical mobility**. Occupational mobility would mean changing trade, labour turnover is the rate at which workers leave a firm, and unemployment means having no job. **Answer: A.**

enonce_markdown:
The table shows the daily demand for and supply of casual workers in a town.

| Wage (FCFA per day) | Workers demanded | Workers supplied |
|---|---|---|
| 2,000 | 900 | 300 |
| 3,000 | 700 | 500 |
| 4,000 | 500 | 700 |
| 5,000 | 300 | 900 |

The government introduces a minimum wage of 5,000 FCFA per day. How many workers are unemployed as a result? (Assume the equilibrium wage is below 5,000.)
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A minimum wage set above the equilibrium wage is a price floor. At that wage the labour supplied is greater than the labour demanded, and the difference is unemployment.

### Solution

At 5,000 FCFA: workers supplied = 900 and workers demanded = 300.

Unemployment $= 900 - 300 = 600$.

The figure 300 is only the number employed, 900 is the number of workers seeking jobs, and 1,200 adds the two columns. **Answer: B.**

enonce_markdown: A nurse earning 2,000 FCFA per hour works 40 hours a week. When her hourly wage rises to 3,000 FCFA she decides to work only 35 hours a week. Which statement best explains her decision?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A higher wage has two effects: the substitution effect (leisure becomes more costly, so work more) and the income effect (she is richer, so she can afford more leisure). At high wages the income effect can dominate.

### Solution

Her hours fell although the wage rose. This happens when the **income effect is stronger than the substitution effect**: she can reach her target income with fewer hours and chooses more leisure. This produces the backward-bending part of the labour supply curve.

If the substitution effect were stronger she would have worked more hours. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: The substitution effect is stronger than the income effect.
The firm has reduced its demand for her labour.
The income effect is stronger than the substitution effect.
The wage is now below the equilibrium wage.

enonce_markdown:
A tailor is paid 600 FCFA for each school uniform he finishes. During one week he finishes 18, 20, 22, 19 and 21 uniforms on the five working days.

(a) Calculate his earnings for the week. (2 marks)

(b) His employer is considering paying him a time rate of 10,000 FCFA per day instead. Calculate his weekly earnings under that method. (1 mark)

(c) State one advantage of a piece rate to the employer and one advantage of a time rate to the worker. (2 marks)
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Under a piece rate, earnings = output times rate per unit. Under a time rate, earnings = rate times time worked, whatever the output.

### Solution

**(a)** Total output $= 18 + 20 + 22 + 19 + 21 = 100$ uniforms. Earnings $= 100 \times 600 = 60\,000$ FCFA.

**(b)** Time rate: $5 \times 10\,000 = 50\,000$ FCFA.

**(c)** Piece rate, advantage to the employer: it gives the worker a reason to produce more, and the cost of labour per unit is fixed, so there is little need for supervision. Time rate, advantage to the worker: income is steady and certain, even in a week when output is low or materials run out.

A furniture workshop sells each chair for 1,000 FCFA. The table shows how many chairs each additional worker produces per day.

| Worker | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th | 5th | 6th | 7th |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Extra chairs | 14 | 12 | 10 | 8 | 6 | 4 | 2 |

The daily wage is 7,000 FCFA per worker. How many workers will the workshop employ if it wants to maximise profit?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The marginal revenue product (MRP) of labour is the extra revenue from one more worker: extra output times price. A profit-maximising firm hires workers as long as MRP is at least equal to the wage.

### Solution

MRP of each worker $=$ extra chairs $\times 1\,000$: 14,000; 12,000; 10,000; 8,000; 6,000; 4,000; 2,000 FCFA.

The 4th worker adds 8,000 FCFA, which is above the wage of 7,000, so he is worth hiring. The 5th adds only 6,000, which is below the wage. The firm therefore employs **4 workers**.

Choosing 7 means hiring everybody; choosing 5 or 6 means hiring workers whose MRP is below the wage. **Answer: A.**
